title: Senior Alert
subtitle: Risk assessment and care planning at the point of care

slides.title: Senior Alert
slides.standfirst: A decision support application for adult risk assessment and preventive care planning, designed to live inside several different electronic medical record systems rather than alongside them.

bullets.text: UX Lead
One of Sweden's ~100 national quality registers
Sustained co-design with clinicians, weekly

slides.notes: Open with the register, not the app. Senior Alert is national infrastructure; the software is the part that either feeds it or does not.

slides.title: Five preventive risk areas for elderly patients
slides.standfirst: Identify who is at risk before the harm happens, and the preventive working method raises the chance of best-possible care regardless of who provides it.

figure.caption: Five areas, one assessment, performed at the point of care

callout.text: One of Sweden's roughly 100 national quality registers, and the preventive working method behind it raises the possibility of best-possible care regardless of who provides it.

slides.notes: Name all five out loud. It makes concrete what "preventive risk assessment" means to anyone who has not worked in Swedish elderly care.

slides.title: A register only works if the assessment actually gets completed during care
slides.standfirst: And the assessment sat outside the systems clinicians worked in.

bullets.text: Leaving the EMR to open a separate tool puts documentation in direct competition with patient contact.
That is a reliable way to lose data — not because clinicians are careless, but because the patient is in front of them.
Missing assessments are not a compliance problem. They are missing preventive care.

callout.text: Not only design a usable assessment interface, but deliver one that could be embedded inside different EMR systems.

slides.notes: The competition framing is the whole argument. Documentation loses to patient contact every time, so the tool has to stop asking clinicians to choose.

slides.title: Four stages, clinicians embedded throughout
slides.standfirst: Not consulted at review points — present in the work, every week.
slides.notes: Emphasise "embedded". This project's quality comes almost entirely from cadence rather than from any single method.

slides.title: Role-differentiated, because the same assessment means something different to each role

bullets.text: At a healthcare centre.
On-site, with a group of clinicians.
Primary care nurses.
Specialist physicians.
The process manager at the hospital.
Two patients.
Iterative online feedback, so designs never drifted far from clinical reality.

slides.notes: Thirteen engagements total. The patient interview matters disproportionately — patients experience the preventive process downstream, and nobody else in the room could speak for that.

slides.title: The focus group output became a service blueprint
slides.standfirst: Mapping actions, frontstage, backstage and support exposed where the assessment actually sat in the care process — and what had to happen invisibly behind it.

lanes.name: Physical evidence
steps: Tablet running Nova, and the QR

lanes.name: Actions
steps: Determining who is going to perform the assessment
Meeting the patient, asking the questions, performing the assessment
Going to the computer and running the SA app

lanes.name: Front of stage
steps: Writing the answers on the paper forms
Selecting the risk assessment area, filling in the values for each element

slides.notes: Walk the vertical, not the horizontal: at each stage, ask what the clinician sees versus what the systems are doing. The paper-forms step in stage two is the one to dwell on.

slides.title: Paper was the bridge, and the bridge was the failure point
slides.standfirst: Answers were captured on paper at the bedside, then re-entered at a computer afterwards. Two acts of documentation for one assessment.

bullets.text: Every step between the bedside and the keyboard is a chance for the assessment to never arrive.
The backstage lane was where the value was: summation, care plan generation, journal writing, discharge report, QR update — all invisible to the clinician.
So the design target was to make the invisible half do more, and the clinician-facing half ask less.

slides.title: Designing something that has to live inside someone else's system
slides.standfirst: The application could not assume control of its own container.

bullets.text: Partly determined by the host record system.
Which patient, which encounter — supplied, not chosen.
Whatever that particular EMR was willing to expose.

callout.text: Reconcile primary care nurses, specialist physicians, hospital process managers and patients, each with a different relationship to the same assessment.

slides.notes: Two constraints at right angles: technical containment and audience spread. The blueprint was the only artefact that held both at once.

bullets.text: The assessment renders in the clinician's existing context.
Values entered once, summed and summarised by the app.
The individual care plan is added automatically, then written to the journal.
So the paper bridge stops being necessary.

slides.title: Three decisions that carried the project

cards.title: Blueprint before interface
cards.text: Mapping frontstage, backstage and support first meant the interface was designed against the real process rather than against the assessment form.

cards.title: Weekly, not milestone
cards.text: A weekly online feedback cycle with clinicians made drift impossible. Nothing got a month of momentum before someone who does the work saw it.

cards.title: Integration as a design constraint
cards.text: Treating the EMR as the container from day one — rather than as a deployment detail — is why it could be embedded across different record systems.

slides.notes: If the audience takes one thing, make it the first card. Blueprint before interface is transferable to any embedded clinical tool.

slides.notes: Thirteen engagements across four professional roles plus patients, on a project of this size, is the number worth pausing on.

slides.title: If documentation competes with patient contact, documentation loses
slides.standfirst: The design job in clinical software is rarely to make the form nicer. It is to remove the moment where a clinician has to choose between the patient and the record.

callout.text: The most valuable work happened below the line of visibility — summation, care plan generation, journal writing, discharge reporting. Nobody sees it, and it is the reason the assessment gets done.

slides.notes: End here. It reframes the whole deck: the visible interface was the smaller half of the design.
